nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What are socio-scientific issues (SSIs) in the context of SSIBL?
nodes.answer: In the context of SSIBL, socio-scientific issues (SSIs) refer to Anthropocene challenges, particularly the dilemma between scientific and technical development and societal change.
nodes.paragraph: This project proposed a teaching and training model named the socioscientific inquiry-based learning model (SSIBL), grounded on three teaching concepts socio- scientific issues (SSIs), inquiry-based science education, and civic literacy education. In this model, SSIs, as the learning context, usually refer to Anthropocene challenges, which include the dilemma between scientific and technical development and societal change. Thus, infusing SSIs into the classroom is envisaged as a crucial aspect of future science education if it is to equip students with the competencies to respond to the vari- ous challenges they will meet in an uncertain future. SSI-based teaching and learning have demonstrated a variety of positive effects on students science learning, including science content (Badeo & Duque, 2022), decision- making (Authors, 2021), environmental NOS views (Herman, 2018), and moral sensi- tivity (Fowler et al., 2009), etc. However, the integration of SSI into science education presents several challenges. According to Zeidler et al. (2019), SSI education should ideally engage students in controversial and ill-structured problems that require interdis- ciplinary thinking and evidence-based reasoning.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Innovation promotion|Sustainable solutions_qna_001
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: According to Jerneck et al. (2011), what dual focus should the field of sustainability science strive for?
nodes.answer: The field must strive to be both problem-solving and critical.
nodes.paragraph: It has emerged as a field attempting to corral numerous interconnected dis- ciplines and fields of study under an umbrella of scholar - ship that seeks to analyze environmental changes and related concerns, better comprehend the causes and consequences of these concerns, and provide avenues and strategies that encourage socioecological sustainability (Clark 2007; Kates et al. 2001). The last aspect is noteworthy. Scholarship in sustainability science is primarily use inspired (Kates 2011) and illuminates the need for developing and implementing solutions to environmental problems. Despite recognition that many environmental problems constitute grand societal challenges, much theoretical development in the field has focused on meso-level analyti- cal tools (e.g., K hler et al. 2019). In recent years, sustain- ability science has seen a shift toward greater emphasis on transformative change (Sahle et al. 2024a, b), necessitat- ing theories and methods that can expose deeper, structural drivers of sustainability problems and inform strategies to address them (Harnesk and Isgren 2021). Jerneck et al. (2011) were early to make clear that the field must strive to be both problem-solving and critical.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What challenge does the paper address regarding the application of certain approaches in sustainability science?
nodes.answer: The paper addresses the challenge that the potential contributions of certain approaches have been limited due to their often neglected, misunderstood, or superficially applied dimensions in sustainability science.
nodes.paragraph: 2021 ). But there is also a tendency in the field to neglect decades and even centuries of theoretical traditions and method- ological efforts to analyze and apprehend the world we inhabit (Longo et al. 2021a, b). While it can be tempting to dismiss long-standing traditions because of their appar - ent failure to do something about problems that persist, like climate change (e.g., O Brien 2016), we start from a rather modest, sociologically informed position regard- ing the relationship between science and societal change. We propose that some existing approaches, such as those which we will elaborate here, have crucial dimensions that often get neglected, misunderstood, or superficially applied, which has limited their potential contributions to sustainability science. Rectifying this does not guarantee that sufficient action will follow but the possibilities to produce well-targeted actions are enhanced. The objective of this paper is to clarify the analytical contributions, and we argue the necessity, of incorporat - ing specific critical theoretical/philosophical traditions into sustainability science: namely, critical realism and historical materialism. While scholars within the field may be familiar with (and have employed) the elements of either or both, they have not yet been brought together and articulated into a distinct sustainability science approach.

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What distinguishes sustainability science from other fields of research?
nodes.answer: Sustainability science is problem and solution-oriented rather than simply curiosity-driven, focusing on facilitating practical sustainability transformations.
nodes.paragraph: This foundation offers a unique approach for critical sustainability science. A sustainability science that takes (critical) realism seriously Sustainability science has been defined as a field of research interested in understanding the interactions between natural and social systems with the aim of facilitating sustainabil- ity transformations (Kates 2011). Other traits ascribed to the field relate to how it is problem and solution oriented as opposed to simply curiosity-driven (Doran et al. 2017 ; Spangenberg 2011), as evidenced by its namesake journal foregrounding the promotion of science-based predic- tions in its description of scope (Springer Nature 2023). Yet, the value proposition for theory in sustainability sci- ence remains questionable at best (Schl ter et al. 2022). It is our contention that sustainability transitions and transfor - mations, especially those capable of tackling today S grand challenges (e.g., climate change, food security, biodiversity loss), require explicit support from an explicit philosophy of science and related social theory. We arrive at this position through a commitment to the principles of realism critical realism, to be precise (Bhaskar 2013).
